## Solution

**Claim.** The $p$-norm and $q$-norm on $C[0,1]$ are equivalent if and only if $p = q$ (with $p,q \in [1,\infty]$).

Here $\|f\|_r = \bigl(\int_0^1 |f(x)|^r\,dx\bigr)^{1/r}$ for $1 \le r < \infty$ and $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{[0,1]}|f|$.

---

### The case $p = q$ is trivial

If $p = q$ the two norms are identical, hence equivalent.

### Setup for $p \neq q$

Two norms $\|\cdot\|_p, \|\cdot\|_q$ are equivalent iff there exist $c, C > 0$ with
$$c\,\|f\|_p \;\le\; \|f\|_q \;\le\; C\,\|f\|_p \qquad \forall\, f \in C[0,1].$$

Since $[0,1]$ has Lebesgue measure $1$, for $1 \le r \le s \le \infty$ and any measurable $f$,
$$\|f\|_r \;\le\; \|f\|_s,$$
because $|f|^s = |f|^r\cdot|f|^{s-r}\le |f|^r\|f\|_\infty^{s-r}$ gives, after integrating, $\|f\|_s \ge \|f\|_r$ on a probability space (equivalently Jensen's inequality $\varphi(t)=t^{s/r}$ convex applied to $|f|^r$). Thus one of the two inequalities always holds for free (the one with the smaller index on the larger side). The obstruction is always the **reverse** inequality: bounding the larger-index norm by the smaller-index norm.

It suffices to show: **for $1 \le r < s \le \infty$ there is no constant $C$ with $\|f\|_s \le C\|f\|_r$ for all $f \in C[0,1]$.** Applying this with $(r,s)=(p,q)$ when $p<q$ kills $\|f\|_q\le C\|f\|_p$; applying it with $(r,s)=(q,p)$ when $q<p$ kills $\|f\|_p\le C\|f\|_q$. Either way equivalence fails.

### The spike construction

Fix $1 \le r < s < \infty$. For each integer $n \ge 1$ define the triangular spike
$$f_n(x) = n^{1/r}\,(1 - nx)\quad\text{for }0\le x\le \tfrac1n,\qquad f_n(x)=0\quad\text{for }x\ge \tfrac1n.$$
Each $f_n$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ (it vanishes at $x=1/n$), non-negative, with $f_n(0)=n^{1/r}$.

**Compute $\|f_n\|_r$.** Substituting $u = nx$,
$$\|f_n\|_r^r = \int_0^{1/n} n\,(1-nx)^r\,dx = \int_0^1 (1-u)^r\,du = \frac{1}{r+1}.$$
Hence $\|f_n\|_r = (r+1)^{-1/r}$, **bounded independently of $n$**.

**Compute $\|f_n\|_s$.**
$$\|f_n\|_s^s = \int_0^{1/n} n^{s/r}(1-nx)^s\,dx = n^{s/r-1}\int_0^1(1-u)^s\,du = \frac{n^{s/r-1}}{s+1}.$$
Thus
$$\|f_n\|_s = (s+1)^{-1/s}\, n^{\,\frac{s/r-1}{s}} = (s+1)^{-1/s}\, n^{\,1/r - 1/s}.$$
Since $r < s$, the exponent $\tfrac1r - \tfrac1s > 0$, so
$$\|f_n\|_s \;\longrightarrow\; \infty \qquad (n\to\infty),$$
while $\|f_n\|_r$ stays bounded. Therefore no constant $C$ can satisfy $\|f\|_s \le C\|f\|_r$ on $C[0,1]$.

### The case $s = \infty$

For $1 \le r < \infty$, use the spikes $g_n(x) = 1 - nx$ on $[0,1/n]$, $0$ elsewhere. Then $\|g_n\|_\infty = 1$ for all $n$, but
$$\|g_n\|_r^r = \int_0^{1/n}(1-nx)^r\,dx = \frac{1}{n(r+1)} \;\longrightarrow\; 0.$$
So $\|g_n\|_\infty / \|g_n\|_r = \bigl(n(r+1)\bigr)^{1/r}\to\infty$: no constant $C$ gives $\|f\|_\infty \le C\|f\|_r$.

### Conclusion

- If $p = q$: norms identical, equivalent. ✓
- If $p < q$: $\|f\|_p \le \|f\|_q$ holds (measure $1$), but $\|f\|_q \le C\|f\|_p$ fails by the spike with $(r,s)=(p,q)$. ✗
- If $q < p$: $\|f\|_q \le \|f\|_p$ holds, but $\|f\|_p \le C\|f\|_q$ fails by the spike with $(r,s)=(q,p)$. ✗

Hence the $p$-norm and $q$-norm on $C[0,1]$ are equivalent **if and only if $p = q$**.
